edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter VII, printed pp. 46-47 (PDF pages 70-71)

source_text:
Quod porro anima nostra rationis sit particeps, multis argumentis ostendi potest: ac primum quidem, ex eo, quod artes vitae nostrae utiles ipsa adinvenerit. Neque enim eas temere, aut casu aliquo repertas esse, quis dixerit: cum nec otiosas, nec vitae inutiles easdem esse, queat demonstrare. Si igitur artes ad vitae utilitatem conferunt; et quae sunt utilia, etiam laudabilia sunt; laudabilia vero ratione comparentur; animae vero inventa, ipsae sint artes: Anima igitur nostra, rationis est particeps.

Deinde ex eo, quod sensus nostri ad res comprehendendas non sunt sufficientes, etiam animam nostram ratione praeditam esse demonstratur. Neque enim sola sensus applicatione, valemus ad res cognoscendas pervenire. At quia nec in hisce volumus inhaerere, id protinus inde constat, quod sensus, nisi ratione adiuventur, ea, quae figura sunt aequalia, et colore similia, natura tamen differentia, internoscere atque discernere nequeant. Quapropter, cum sensus ratione destituti, falsas nobis rerum imagines ac species inducant; reputandum nobis est, res comprehendi ne revera queant, necne: et si quidem comprehendi possunt, alia nobis praeter sensus vis est, eaque praestantior, qua ad earum cognitionem pervenire liceat. Quod si non comprehenduntur; ne illa quidem assequi poterimus, quae aliter quam sunt, conspiciuntur. Res porro a nobis percipi, vel ex eo patet, quod eas convenienter ad usus nostros adhibemus, et rursus in quodcunque volumus, convertimus. Quare si res comprehendi posse, a nobis demonstratum est; idque a sensibus ratione destitutis effici nequeat, quippe qui falsas nobis opiniones repraesentant; mens sane erit, quae ratione cuncta distinguit atque diiudicat, et res ut revera sunt, cognoscit: mens autem est Animae pars ratione decorata ac illustrata. Est ergo Anima rationis particeps.

Postremo, quia nihil agimus, quod non prius nobis ipsi descripserimus atque definierimus: id autem nihil aliud est, quam animae dignitas: quippe cui non extrinsecus advenit rerum cognitio, sed ipsa tanquam suis commentis ac sensis res ornat. et ideo in seipsa rem ante depingit atque describit, ut sic eam postea in medium proferat. Animae porro dignitas, nihil aliud est, quam ratione omnia facere, qua quidem etiam a sensibus differt. Animam igitur ratione praeditam esse, iam demonstratum est.
orientation: Three arguments close the treatise by showing that the soul shares in reason: it discovered the useful arts, the senses alone cannot judge things truly, and the soul plans within itself before it acts.
pass_a_gloss: That moreover our soul is a sharer of reason (rationis particeps) can be shown by many arguments (argumentis); and first from this, that it itself discovered (adinvenerit) the arts (artes) useful (utiles) to our life. For who would say they were found (repertas) rashly (temere) or by some chance (casu), since one cannot (queat) demonstrate that they are idle (otiosas) or useless to life? If therefore the arts contribute (conferunt) to the usefulness of life; and things that are useful are also praiseworthy (laudabilia); and praiseworthy things are acquired (comparentur) by reason; and the arts themselves are inventions (inventa) of the soul: our soul therefore is a sharer of reason. Next, from this, that our senses (sensus) are not sufficient (sufficientes) for grasping (comprehendendas) things, it is also demonstrated that our soul is endowed (praeditam) with reason. For by the application (applicatione) of sense alone we are not able (valemus) to arrive at knowing things. But that we do not wish (volumus) to cling (inhaerere) to these, this is at once (protinus) evident from this, that the senses, unless they are helped (adiuventur) by reason, cannot discern and distinguish (internoscere atque discernere) things which are equal in shape (figura aequalia) and alike in color (colore similia) yet differing in nature (natura differentia). Wherefore, since the senses deprived (destituti) of reason bring in (inducant) to us false images and appearances (imagines ac species) of things, we must reckon (reputandum) whether things can truly (revera) be grasped or not; and if indeed they can be grasped, there is in us another power (vis) besides the senses, and that more excellent (praestantior), by which it is permitted (liceat) to arrive at the knowledge (cognitionem) of them. But if they are not grasped, we shall not be able to attain (assequi) even those things which are seen (conspiciuntur) otherwise than they are. Moreover, that things are perceived by us is evident even from this, that we apply (adhibemus) them suitably (convenienter) to our uses, and again turn (convertimus) them into whatever we wish. Therefore if it has been demonstrated by us that things can be grasped, and this cannot be effected by the senses destitute of reason, since they represent (repraesentant) false opinions (opiniones) to us, it will surely (sane) be the mind (mens) which distinguishes and judges (distinguit atque diiudicat) all things by reason, and knows things as they truly are; and the mind is the part (pars) of the soul adorned and illuminated (decorata ac illustrata) with reason. Therefore the soul is a sharer of reason. Lastly, because we do nothing which we have not first described and defined (descripserimus atque definierimus) for ourselves; and this is nothing other than the dignity (dignitas) of the soul; since to it knowledge of things does not come from outside (extrinsecus advenit), but it itself, as it were with its own devisings and conceptions (commentis ac sensis), adorns (ornat) things; and therefore in itself it first paints and describes (depingit atque describit) the thing, so that thus it may afterward bring it forth into the midst (in medium proferat). The dignity of the soul, moreover, is nothing other than to do all things by reason, by which indeed it also differs from the senses. That the soul is endowed with reason, therefore, has now been demonstrated.

pass_b_english: Further, that our soul shares in reason can be shown by many arguments. First, from the fact that the soul itself discovered the arts that are useful to our life. For no one would say that they were found at random or by some chance, since no one could show that they are idle or useless to life. If, then, the arts contribute to the benefit of life; and useful things are also praiseworthy; and praiseworthy things are gained by reason; and the arts themselves are discoveries of the soul: then our soul shares in reason.

Next, it is also shown that our soul is endowed with reason from the fact that our senses are not sufficient for grasping things. For we cannot come to know things by the mere application of the senses. And that we do not wish to stop at the senses is plain at once from this: unless reason helps them, the senses cannot tell apart and distinguish things that are equal in shape and alike in color but different in nature. Since, then, the senses without reason bring false images and forms of things before us, we must consider whether things can truly be grasped or not. If they can be grasped, we have another power besides the senses, and a higher one, by which we may come to know them. But if they are not grasped, we shall not be able to reach even those things that are seen otherwise than they are. That things are perceived by us is clear, if from nothing else, from the fact that we put them fittingly to our uses and turn them again into whatever we wish. So if we have shown that things can be grasped, and this cannot be done by the senses without reason, since they set false notions before us, then it will surely be the mind that distinguishes and judges all things by reason and knows things as they truly are. And the mind is the part of the soul adorned and enlightened with reason. The soul, therefore, shares in reason.

Finally, it is shown from the fact that we do nothing that we have not first sketched out and defined for ourselves; and this is nothing other than the dignity of the soul. For knowledge of things does not come to it from outside; rather, it adorns things, as it were, with its own designs and conceptions, and so it first paints and sketches a thing within itself, so that it may afterward bring it out into the open. The dignity of the soul, moreover, is nothing other than doing all things by reason, and by this it also differs from the senses. It has now been shown, therefore, that the soul is endowed with reason.
notes: Edition chapter VII ('An rationis particeps nostra sit Anima'); end of the treatise.
'rationis particeps' rendered 'shares in reason' and 'ratione praedita' 'endowed with reason'; the plan in section 1 calls this question 'rational or lacking in reason', hence the title.

Doubtful reading: 'At quia nec in hisce volumus inhaerere' ('volumus' clear in the print, rechecked on the page image, PDF p. 70; 'valemus' would give 'we are not able to rest in them') rendered as printed, 'that we do not wish to stop at the senses', with 'quia' taken as 'that' and 'hisce' as the senses.

'ne illa quidem assequi poterimus, quae aliter quam sunt, conspiciuntur' rendered closely; the sense appears to be that if nothing could be grasped we could not even recognize that some things appear otherwise than they are.
'comparentur' (subjunctive) treated as one more premise of the 'if' chain.
'ornat' kept as 'adorns'; 'commentis ac sensis' rendered 'designs and conceptions'.

Margin variants (blurred, uncertain) not adopted: 'al. aspectu tamen' at 'natura tamen' ('different in appearance'); 'al. quae omnem rationem discernit' at 'quae ratione cuncta distinguit'; and at 'qua quidem etiam a sensibus differt' the alternative 'haec enim etiam a sensibus differre demonstratum est. Anima igitur ratione praedita est.' 'et ideo' after a full stop joined to the preceding sentence in the English.
